prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength to reach fractional uncertainties near 10^-18.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B030 alone, credited to Katori and Ye. After the full exchange, the point that settles the overlap worry for me is that the 2005 prize honoured the optical frequency comb and the 2012 prize honoured quantum control of single trapped ions, whereas this prize honours a different idea: cancelling the lattice light shift at a magic wavelength so that many neutral atoms can be interrogated at once without Doppler or recoil limits. That can be said in one sentence, and I would accept it as the committee's answer to the chair's first question. The physics that follows (forbidden transitions, light shifts, controlled many-body shifts) is the achievement itself and not only engineering, and the payoff is the kind of clue from nature I value as a theorist: millimetre-scale redshift tests, bounds on varying constants and ultralight dark matter. Independent agreement near 1e-18 among laboratories in several countries establishes maturity, and the two-name credit needs no arbitrary cut. I would write the citation around the magic-wavelength invention and its realization, not around timekeeping in general and not around the redefinition of the second.
statement.case_against: The overlap with earlier metrology prizes remains my strongest reservation, but I now regard it as a matter of how the citation is worded and not as disqualifying. A bare 'optical clocks' citation would invite exactly the third-prize-for-one-lineage reading. Remaining weaknesses are that this is an instrument and method achievement whose discovery content is argued through what it enables, that Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow and the ion-clock groups lie outside the two names, and that I cannot verify the priority history from the supplied text. If a majority judged that the metrology record is saturated, B020 is the cleaner discovery and I would say so, but I do not hold that view.

responses.point: Mehlig keeps B030 first but says the method overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is close enough that it should not be treated as closed, and that the pending redefinition affects how much practical impact is already realised.
responses.response: I share your caution and I would not treat the overlap as closed by assertion. My answer to the chair is that the one-sentence distinction above does the work: the earlier prizes gave us a ruler for optical frequencies and control of single ions, and neither contained the magic-wavelength lattice that lets many neutral atoms act as one clock. Your own point that ensemble averaging beats quantum projection noise and that many-body shifts must be controlled is the best evidence that this is new physics. On the redefinition, I agree the biggest payoff is prospective, but the case does not need it: 1e-18 agreement between laboratories is already demonstrated, and that is what I would ask the committee to record.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B022 (Parrinello and Car) alone for its clean two-name credit and forty years of use, names B030 as his first alternative, and says he would not stand in the way of B030 on the merits.
responses.response: I respect the clarity of the Car-Parrinello credit and I agree it is as clean as B030. My difficulty is disciplinary and about the kind of achievement. Ab initio molecular dynamics is a computational method whose effect is felt mostly in chemistry and materials science, and only you and Mehlig ranked it highly. I also note your disclosure that this is your own field, which argues for you stepping back from weighing it. Since you say you would not oppose B030 and would defer to the atomic-physics colleagues on priority, I would ask whether you can now state B030 as your single preferred part. I have not placed B022 among my alternatives, because I think it would not gather votes as a physics prize.

responses.point: Kroll argues the 2005 and 2012 prizes did not cover a neutral-atom lattice clock, and that the citation must honour the invention and its realization rather than a series of performance records, since Ye's record accuracy partly refines an existing concept.
responses.response: I agree with both points and the second is a useful discipline for the citation. It is why I prefer the magic-wavelength wording that you also support, which anchors Katori's proposal and the realization of the many-atom clock, over wording that celebrates a particular accuracy number. I would keep 'near 10^-18' only as a description of what the realization achieved. On B004 we have already disagreed about dropping Greiner. I take your admission that you would not defend your own trio against Bloch, Greiner and Zoller as confirming that its allocation is not settled enough to make B004 a preferred part, and I would not add a second prize part to B030 on that basis.

responses.point: Lindroth holds that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct concept that neither prize covered, would not name Lemonde in the citation, and treats the pending redefinition of the second as a timing question and not a flaw in the science.
responses.response: This is the framing I now adopt. Because you are closest to the atomic physics, your view that the two-name allocation holds up against Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow and the ion-clock groups carries more weight with me than my own recollection. What I would need from the committee's experts before the vote is confirmation that the magic-wavelength proposal and the early lattice demonstrations belong to Katori, and that the controlled many-body regime and record accuracy belong to Ye, with Lemonde's independent proposal treated as a contested neighbouring contribution and not a clear omission. I agree the redefinition should not delay the award: the case rests on demonstrated performance.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, keeps B020 as his first alternative and says the better case would be IceCube if the committee wanted a new observational window and judged the attribution gap smaller.
responses.response: I opened with B020 as my first choice, so I understand the pull, and I would still support it as the fallback if B030 were set aside. On credit, my view has moved a little: Spiering belongs in a three-name set, but the split among AMANDA founders, IceCube leaders and the collaboration is less settled than for Katori and Ye, and the origin of most of the diffuse flux is still unresolved. If B030 stalls on the overlap objection, I would turn to B020 with Halzen, Karle and Spiering before B004, but I would not combine the two parts now, because a second part with an open allocation weakens the configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the one-sentence distinction from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 trapped-ion prizes, and whether the citation should name the magic wavelength explicitly.

Whether Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow or other lattice-clock contributors should be considered within the credited names; I rely on Lindroth and Kroll for the priority history and have not checked it independently.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should delay the award; I think not, but I cannot confirm its current status from the supplied material.
If B030 is set aside, my fallback is B020 with Halzen, Karle and Spiering, but I am not confident in the credit allocation there.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my disclosure. No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B030, B020 or B004. My documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group) are not linked to the credited names. Eriksson and I are both at Uppsala, but I have no tie to B022 and no role in it.
